summary: Describes how to use PKCS #12 (RFC 7292) to carry key containers (PFX) holding keys and certificates when using the Russian national GOST algorithms. It was developed outside the IETF and published to help interoperable implementations; it does not imply IETF endorsement.

plainLanguage.summary: A PFX file is like a locked box for keys. This says how to build that box when using Russia's national lock designs, so different programs can open each other's boxes.

subtitle: How to package GOST cryptographic keys and certificates for secure storage and exchange.

tldr.problem: Organizations using Russian national cryptographic standards (GOST algorithms) need a standard way to securely store and transport private keys and certificates, similar to how other organizations use PKCS #12 containers with conventional algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9548 specifies how to use PKCS #12 (a standard for key containers, also called PFX files) with GOST R 34.10-2012 (a Russian national elliptic curve signature algorithm) and GOST R 34.11-2012 (a Russian national hash function). Keys are masked for side-channel protection, encrypted with password-based key derivation, and the container is authenticated with HMAC.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can now securely exchange GOST-protected keys and certificates using the standardized PFX format, enabling interoperability between implementations. The specification does not imply IETF endorsement of the GOST algorithms.

today: RFC 9548 is an Informational document published by the RFC Editor as an independent contribution. It defines how to use PKCS #12 with GOST algorithms to enable interoperable implementations in Russia and other countries using GOST as national standards. The document does not establish IETF standards or imply endorsement of GOST algorithms by the IETF.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
PKCS #12 is a widely used standard for securing and transporting cryptographic keys and certificates. It defines a format called PFX (Personal Information eXchange) that can hold private keys, public key certificates, and other secrets, all protected by a password.

This RFC explains how to use PKCS #12 with the GOST cryptographic algorithms, which are national standards of Russia. GOST R 34.10-2012 is an elliptic curve signature algorithm, and GOST R 34.11-2012 is a hash function. The specification was developed outside the IETF to enable interoperable implementations. It is important to note that neither the IETF nor the IRTF has analyzed GOST for security weaknesses, and this RFC does not constitute IETF endorsement of these algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: Just like you can save your keys in different types of safes, cryptographic keys can be stored in different formats. This document explains how to store Russian cryptographic keys in the PFX safe.

sections.title: PFX Structure and Containers
sections.content:
A PFX file contains an AuthenticatedSafe, which is a sequence of contents that can be encrypted or unencrypted, followed by optional MacData for integrity protection. The AuthenticatedSafe is organized into SafeBags, each of which holds one object such as a private key (pkcs8ShroudedKeyBag) or a certificate (certBag).

When using GOST algorithms with password protection, private keys are encrypted using the PBES2 (Password-Based Encryption Scheme 2) algorithm defined in RFC 9337. The entire PFX structure is authenticated using an HMAC calculated from the GOST R 34.11-2012 hash function, allowing recipients to verify that the container has not been tampered with.
sections.plainLanguage: A PFX file is like a folder inside a safe: the folder has pockets for keys and certificates, and the whole thing is locked with a password and sealed with a tamper-proof mark.

sections.title: Key Representation and Masking
sections.content:
GOST R 34.10-2012 keys can be represented in two forms. A 256-bit key is stored as a 64-byte value (two 32-byte coordinates). A 512-bit key is stored as a 128-byte value (two 64-byte coordinates). Keys are encoded in little-endian format.

To protect private keys from side-channel attacks (such as power analysis), the RFC specifies key masking. A private key can be masked by multiplying it by the inverse of one or more random masks in the field. The masked key, along with the masks themselves, are stored in the PFX container. When the key is needed, the masks are removed by multiplication (unmask operation). Masking increases security against attacks that observe power consumption or electromagnetic emissions during key operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine hiding a secret by mixing it with random numbers so an attacker who watches your computer cannot figure out the real secret. Masking does that with cryptographic keys.

sections.title: Password Encryption and Integrity Protection
sections.content:
The password used to protect a PFX container must be encoded as a Unicode UTF-8 string. This password is processed by the PBKDF2 key derivation function (RFC 9337) along with a random salt to generate encryption and authentication keys. The salt and iteration count are stored in the PFX file so the recipient can regenerate the same keys from the same password.

The same password can be used to encrypt different sections (keys or certificates) with different random salt values, adding security. The integrity of the entire container is verified using HMAC-GOST R 34.11-2012-512, a keyed hash function. Only if the HMAC matches can you be confident the PFX has not been modified.
sections.plainLanguage: Your password is mixed with a random number to create a lock that can encrypt and seal the box. The random number is saved so you can unlock the exact same lock with the same password later.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements and Interoperability
sections.content:
Implementations MUST use the PBES2 scheme for encrypting private keys and MUST NOT use unencrypted formats unless explicitly required. Key masking SHOULD be used to protect against side-channel attacks. The salt (initialization value) SHOULD contain at least 32 octets of random data to reduce the chance of accidental collisions.

The RFC provides detailed ASN.1 module definitions and concrete examples of PFX containers with GOST keys and certificates in appendices. These examples show both password-protected keys with unencrypted certificates and password-protected keys with password-protected certificates, enabling developers to verify their implementations against known test vectors.
sections.plainLanguage: The document includes step-by-step examples so programmers can test their code: "here is a sample box, here is how to open it."

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that masked keys should be used to protect against side-channel attacks during key reading and operations. Passwords must be stored securely and protected from disclosure. Each use of PBKDF2 must employ unique random salt values (at least 8 to 32 bytes) to prevent key reuse if two containers are protected with the same password.

The PBES2 scheme must be used for all encryption; unencrypted keys MUST NOT be transported in shared containers. Public keys must be DER-encoded as octet strings per RFC 9215. Implementers are advised to follow RFC 7292 for general PFX security best practices and RFC 9337 for password-based key derivation specifics.
sections.plainLanguage: Use strong random numbers, protect passwords carefully, and always encrypt keys before moving them. These steps keep your cryptographic treasures safe.
